Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes): Acute onset diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days with subjective fever and periumbilical abdominal pain/tenderness; unable to keep fluids down. No chronic medical conditions reported.  
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes): Not recorded.  
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines: Vitamin D — taken every day. Oral rehydration solution (salt-sugar ORS) — taken ~3 times daily for past 2 days. Ibuprofen — occasional for menstrual cramps; dose/route/frequency not documented. No drug allergies documented in transcript.  
- Immunisation status reviewed (flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus): Not recorded.  
- Sexual/reproductive health status and risks: Not on contraception. Not currently sexually active. Last menstrual period ~2 weeks ago. No other sexual/reproductive risks documented.  
- Lifestyle: physical activity, diet, tobacco, alcohol, substance use: Eats normally/well. Does not smoke. Drinks alcohol occasionally (a pint sometimes). No recreational drug use reported. Physical activity not recorded.  
- Hearing and vision concerns: Not recorded.  
- Mood, mental health, and risk assessment (depression, anxiety, self-harm): Not recorded.  
- Social context: family support, caregiving, housing, financial stressors: Lives with brother and mother. Brother has had similar symptoms (household contact). Working as a graphics designer; working from home today due to illness. No other social determinants documented.

- Vital signs: BP, pulse rate and rhythm: Not recorded; no objective vitals recorded.  
- Anthropometry: height, weight, BMI, waist circumference if indicated: Not recorded.  
- Oral health: gums, teeth, dentures if relevant: Not recorded.

- Blood tests: fasting glucose and lipids preferred; HbA1c if diabetes present/suspected: Not recorded.  
- Renal function and liver function tests if clinically indicated: Not recorded.

- Bone density (DEXA) if osteoporosis risk present: Not recorded.  
- Other relevant investigations from encounter: Clinician recommended stool sample for microbiology and in-clinic assessment of hydration. No tests performed yet.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impressions:
  - Acute gastroenteritis presentation: 3 days of watery → very loose diarrhoea, profuse vomiting (cannot retain fluids), subjective high fever, crampy periumbilical pain with localized tenderness reported, household contact with similar illness (brother) and reported school outbreak.
  - Risk of dehydration due to ongoing vomiting and poor oral intake; patient passed urine ~1 hour prior (subjective), suggesting not yet severely dehydrated but at risk.
- Working diagnosis: Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus). Supported by acute onset vomiting and watery diarrhoea, subjective fever, household contact and reported local outbreak (DDx: High likelihood).
- Management plan documented in transcript:
  - Arrange urgent clinic appointment for assessment of hydration and to provide/send stool sample for microbiology (stool culture/PCR) as indicated. (Appointment to be booked via support line as clinician arranged.)
  - Advise continued use of ORS in very small frequent sips to minimize vomiting; patient instructed to persist with small sips continually.
  - Dietary advice: bland/light foods (toast, plain biscuits); avoid fruit, vegetables, milk and similar items that may worsen symptoms.
  - Escalation plan: attend A&E urgently if symptoms worsen or if unable to maintain hydration.
  - Consideration for IV fluids and more urgent intervention if clinical assessment shows dehydration or inability to tolerate oral fluids.
- Considerations from DDx consistent with transcript:
  - Bacterial gastroenteritis — medium likelihood: persistent/worsening symptoms and fever justify stool testing and possible targeted therapy if bacterial pathogen identified.
  - Foodborne toxin (preformed toxin) — medium likelihood: prominent vomiting and possible clustered cases could reflect toxin-mediated food poisoning.
  - Appendicitis — low likelihood: periumbilical tenderness could reflect early appendicitis but presence of diarrhoea, household outbreak, and vomiting favor infectious gastroenteritis.
- Conflict noted: None between transcript and DDx interpretations; both support infectious gastroenteritis as most likely. (No direct contradictions documented.)

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification: Advice given regarding rehydration (ORS small sips) and dietary modification during acute illness. No chronic disease prevention counseling documented.  
- Patient health goals and priorities: Not recorded.  
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA): Not recorded.  
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports): Urgent clinic assessment and stool sample collection recommended. A&E referral advised if clinical deterioration. No other referrals recorded.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled: Urgent clinic appointment to be booked through support line (no date/time recorded). Patient instructed to call/attend sooner if symptoms worsen.

Consider

- Mental health support or counselling referral: Not recorded.  
- Specialist referral for complex chronic disease management: Not recorded.  
- Dental referral if oral health issues identified: Not recorded.  
- Optometry referral for visual concerns or regular screening: Not recorded.  
- Audiometry referral if hearing issues suspected: Not recorded.  
- Social work or housing support referral if social determinants affect health: Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus) — High likelihood. Acute onset watery diarrhoea, profuse vomiting, subjective fever, periumbilical cramps, household contact and local outbreak are classic features supporting this diagnosis.  
- Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, pathogenic E. coli) — Medium likelihood. Fever, ongoing severe diarrhoea and failure to improve with ORS increase the possibility; stool testing recommended to exclude treatable bacterial causes.  
- Foodborne toxin (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) — Medium likelihood. Prominent vomiting and possible clustering/household/school exposure could reflect toxin-mediated food poisoning, though no clear single shared meal was identified.

Quality checks

- Missing but clinically expected elements: No objective vital signs recorded (temperature, BP, heart rate, respiratory rate), no assessment of hydration status documented (skin turgor, mucous membranes, orthostatic vitals), no weight/BMI, no immunisation review, no baseline blood tests (electrolytes/renal function) despite risk for dehydration, no stool test results yet, no documentation of allergies.  
- Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified. DDx and clinician impression are concordant (infectious gastroenteritis most likely).  
- Transcript quality notes: Transcript contains several brief pauses and some incomplete responses; patient lost count of stool frequency. Patient provided name and DOB (4 October 1984) and partial address; some questions had minimal or delayed responses.
